analysis.one_liner: Exempts approved pesticide applications and their residue from Clean Water Act discharge permits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action, so Clean Water Act permitting of pesticide discharges stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal pesticide law and the Clean Water Act to bar the EPA or states from requiring a water pollution permit for discharges of approved pesticides or their residue into navigable waters, even though pesticide sprays routinely drift or run off into rivers and lakes. It carves out exceptions for illegal applications that pollute water, stormwater, industrial effluent, and vessel discharges. It also directs the EPA to report to Congress within a year on how pesticide registration could better protect water quality and human health. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be pesticide users and producers: farms, forestry operations, mosquito and weed control programs, and commercial applicators, who currently face a two-track system — pesticide approval under FIFRA and a separate Clean Water Act permit for spraying into or near water. Pesticide manufacturers would also benefit from fewer permit-related requirements on their products' use.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA or any state from requiring a Clean Water Act permit for discharges of FIFRA-authorized pesticides or their residue resulting from application, eliminating a second layer of federal permitting for pesticide spraying in or near navigable waters.

Keeps permit requirements for genuinely problematic discharges: applications that violate FIFRA provisions protecting water quality, stormwater, manufacturing and industrial effluent, treatment works effluent, and vessel-related discharges.

Requires the EPA, consulting the Agriculture Department, to report to Congress within a year on coordinating water and pesticide program data, the effectiveness of current water-quality protections in pesticide regulation, and how FIFRA could be changed to better protect water quality and health.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on people who drink from, fish in, or recreate in lakes, rivers, and streams: pesticide residue discharged into shared waters would no longer be tracked or controlled through Clean Water Act permits, leaving only pesticide-label review under FIFRA as a safeguard.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who use and drink shared waters

drawbacks.text: The bill removes Clean Water Act permitting as a check on pesticide discharges into navigable waters, meaning pesticide sprays that legally drift or run off into rivers and lakes would face no water-quality permit, monitoring, or reporting requirement at the point of discharge.

FIFRA registration reviews a product's label before sale but was not designed to control where and how much pesticide ends up in a specific body of water, so the remaining safeguard is weaker at the place where pollution actually occurs; the bill itself asks EPA to study whether FIFRA can be modified to better protect water quality, an implicit acknowledgment of that gap.

The bill's real-world cost side is genuine: after a 2011 court ruling, applicators must obtain a general permit in addition to following pesticide labels, and the permit imposes notice, recordkeeping, and treatment-area requirements that fall hardest on small applicators and public agencies like mosquito-control districts — the burden this bill was written to remove.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real compliance burden: spraying an approved pesticide according to its label currently requires a second Clean Water Act permit, which costs time and money for farms, forestry operators, and public mosquito-control programs. But the trade it offers is that legal pesticide applications would enter rivers, lakes, and streams with no point-of-discharge permit, monitoring, or limits at all, leaving water quality to a label-approval system not built for it. Weighing a paperwork saving for applicators against the loss of the only discharge-level control on pesticides in shared waters, the cost side is the heavier one, and the bill's own requirement that EPA study how to better protect water quality under FIFRA suggests its authors knew the substitute was weaker.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in April 2013, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Kay Hagan introduced the bill on April 24, 2013, joined by 13 original cosponsors — 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The committee never reported the bill, and no further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any vote, the existing Clean Water Act permit requirement for pesticide discharges into navigable waters stayed in effect — a win for anyone who uses the affected waters, and a loss for the applicators and manufacturers the bill was written to relieve.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Users of lakes and rivers; permit rules stayed

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans who cosponsored at introduction
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 13 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and its sponsor was a Democrat, so support crossed party lines; opposition never took a recorded form because the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Agricultural and commercial pesticide applicators (farms, forestry, mosquito and weed control)
industries.note: The bill would free them from the separate Clean Water Act permit now required for spraying pesticides into or near waters, saving them notice, recordkeeping, and treatment-area compliance costs. Their gain comes directly from removing the discharge-level check on what ends up in shared waters.

The bill would make FIFRA label approval the sole federal gate for legal pesticide applications in or near navigable waters, relieving their customers of permit requirements and reducing water-quality-based constraints on their products' use.
Communities and industries that rely on untreated or lightly treated surface water would bear more pesticide residue without any permit-based monitoring or limits on legal applications.
